Would anyone happen to know if it is just one warning or if it is missing warnings? Also, if there are 20 warnings that are not displaying, does anyone know how to figure out what they are?

Thanks,

Ryan

I got weird results and I was wondering whether I was coding lavaan correctly...
My metric and configural model differ (delta CFI >.01) so I moved to assess partial invariance using the group.partial option

overall.model=  'latent=~ D1 + D2 + D3+ D4+ D5+ D6+ D7+ D8+ D9+ D10'

temp1 <- cfa(model =  overall.model  ,
            data = mydata,
            meanstructure = TRUE,
            group = "SEX",
            group.equal = c("loadings"),
            group.partial = c("D1=~D1"))

then I run the exact same model but this time group.partial = c("D3=~D3")
then the same model with group.partial = c("D6=~D6") and finally group.partial = c("D1=~D1", "D3=~D3", "D6=~D6")

The problem is that I get the same CFI value with each model. Is it correct what I am doing here? or perhaps instead of group.partial = c("D3=~D3") I should write group.partial = c("latent=~D3").

Thanks.

P.

> > First, am I right to believe that the means and intercepts of latent variables are arbitrary (in my case with the variance of the intercept and slope fixed to 1) and not directly interpretable (e.g. the intercept is not the mean of time point one)?
> > ####
> > the factor means are arbitrary based on the identification method you used. With fixed variance/mean method the means witll be 0 at time 1 and (after strong invariance) for the next times points will be in reference to the mean change compared to time 1. The intercept of growth curve is the average score at which time point you set the 0 in the time scale. This is also arbitrary as you can choose where to set your time 0. But this growth curve is interpretable, most commonly as the mean at the first time point, or start point of the longitudinal change
> >
> > ###
> > Second, I have been asked to compare my linear growth model to intercept-only and curvilinear models to provide a rationale for this approach.
> > ###
> > The intercept only model will be done by excluding any other factor slopes, just one growth factor.
> > The linear model, would have the intercept factor, and the linear slope factors
> > The quadratic model would have, the intercept, linear and quadratic factors
> > Would recommend this book for these other extensions of models
> > Grimm, K. J., Ram, N., & Estabrook, R. (2016). Growth Modeling: Structural Equation and Multilevel Modeling Approaches.
> > A quadratic factor is consider a higher order term. This means that for estimating any higher order terms, you need to include all previous lower order terms, in this case, linear and intercept factors

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, and that is indeed quite a model.   How many variables, and thresholds per ordered variable?  As large as your sample seems, consider how many summary statistics you are trying to reproduce.  A low N-per-statistic is associated with problems estimating the asymptotic covariance matrix of model parameters, from which standard errors are derived (also the weight matrix is derived from the asymptotic covariance matrix of the estimated polychorics/thresholds, so the same issue can manifest in different stages of DWLS estimation).

> I am getting a message that there are 21 warnings. However, when I use "warnings()" to view them, only one is displayed: "In .local(object, ...): lavaan WARNING: fit measures not available if model did not converge."

Perhaps what is happening is that the 21 warnings are accumulated during the sem() call, but then another warning is returned by summary() that clears the previous cache of warnings().  Perhaps you could verify this by calling warnings() immediately after sem().

If this doesn't resolve the issue, you could set options(warn = 1) to print warnings as they occur, then set it back to the default options(warn = 0) after.

messages.subject_clean: partial invariance, right code?
messages.body_plain:
> I was wondering whether I was coding lavaan correctly

You are using the default identification method, where the first factor loadings are fixed to 1.  Thus, they cannot be freed with group.partial=, unless you change the identification to std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE.  In that case, make sure you verify that in the metric-invariance model, the latent variance is freely estimated in all groups except the first.  That has been added in a recent version of lavaan (maybe still in the development version), so you might need to explicitly free the group-2 (and 3, etc.) factor variances manually in the metric model.

latent ~~ c(1, NA)*latent

> My metric and configural model differ (delta CFI >.01)

That is not a test statistic, and it is a poor criteria for making decisions.

 https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000152 (find a copy on my faculty page under Publications)

I recommend using the actual (delta) chi-squared test statistic of the H0 of full invariance.  If it is rejected, you can always make an argument that the amount of DIF (effect size) has little impact on the estimated model parameters (e.g., by comparing estimated latent means/variances between full- and partial-invariance models).

> I get the same CFI value with each model

Within how many digits of precision?  CFI could be nearly the same because each model only reduces the chi-squared by the same relative amount proportional to its df.  And don't use the default baseline model for incremental fit indices, which is not nested in models that constrain means/variances across groups.

https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.8.1.16

https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2014.935928

> the lower bound of the the RMSEA CI is 0.000. The X2 is not significant

There you go.  You cannot reject the H0 of perfect fit with chi-squared, and you also cannot with RMSEA.

> so I should not care about the RMSEA (I think?)

RMSEA's CI allows you to test other H0 values than 0.  Kline's SEM textbook has an example where chi-squared was not significant, but the RMSEA's upper bound also did not allow the H0 of poor fit to be rejected.  Subsequent inspection of correlation residuals showed a large discrepancy between an observed and model-implied correlation, which was just not a large enough effect size to be captured by chi-squared with that N.

> I've also checked local fit indices - i.e., resid(fit, "cor")$cov -  and they do not exceed +1/-1.

 Do you mean +/- 0.1?  That is usually the arbitrary rule of thumb I have seen for classifying an discrepancy as "large enough" to consider of practical importance.

> I think that N = 300 could be one of the reasons why the CI range is large

Its range is affected by both N and df

messages.body_plain:
I think you need to worry about empirical underidentification.  The identification of a 2-indicator factor is tenuous, depending on substantial between-factor correlation(s).  I'm not sure these can be disaggregated from the residual correlations one would normal include in longitudinal CFAs (i.e., correlated specifics), so the tenuous empirical identification could be threatened.

http://ww.w.statpower.net/Steiger%20Biblio/Steiger02.PDF

If your model is empirical identified, negative variance estimates are not necessarily a sign of anything other than sampling error.  You can test the feasibility of that null hypothesis:

https://doi.org/10.1177/0049124112442138

Syntax looks fine, but you don't need to explicitly set ID.fac=, ID.cat=, or group= when you are using the defaults.

> the (residual?) covariances between H7 ~~ H1.7, H7 ~~ H2.7, and H1.7 ~~ H2.7 were negative (-.22 to -.55), although their polychoric correlations (lavCor) are positive. Do you have any suggestions why this happened and whether (and how) it should be fixed?

Nothing to fix.   Residual correlations are partial correlations, given their common predictor(s)/factor(s).  The direction is not bound to match the corresponding zero-order correlation.

>                                return.fit = TRUE)

I would not recommend this.   Better to inspect the syntax object to ensure you are fitting the model you intend to, as the help-page examples show.

> And: the next step would be to set constraints step by step, beginning with long.equal = "thresholds" ?

Yes, assuming you have at least one polytomous indicator per factor.  If one factor has only binary indicators, then you will need to simultaneously constrain thresholds, loadings, and intercepts because binary data cannot distinguish between sources of DIF.  If you have a mix, then all your df to test threshold invariance will simply come from the polytomous indicators.

messages.body_plain:
Others can probably speak to this more proficiently, but when you just request the DWLS estimator without declaring variables as ordered, lavaan doesn't know to treat your variables as ordered; by default, it will treat them as continuous, I believe. So, you will get different results when you simply request the DWLS estimator vs specifically declaring variables as ordered and using the DWLS estimator.

As for the Heywood case, I would guess that it has to do with LV3 having only 2 indicators. Best practice is to have at least 3 indicators per latent factor. In reality, however, that doesn't always work, but when you only have 2 indicators per factor, it can cause issues because that latent variable has to borrow information from other parts of the model to be identified. This might be further complicated by the fact that the items for this factor are binary.

There are a number of posts on the lavaan forum that talk about negative ov variances and most of them point to a 2012 paper in Sociological Methods & Research that discusses how you can look at the 95% confidence interval around the offending estimates to see if it includes plausible values. If it does, then the issue may be due to sampling error rather than model misspecification. Here is a link to post in the forum that might be helpful to you.

messages.subject: Are “EBM” and “regression” equivalent when indicators are categorical?
messages.subject_clean: Are “EBM” and “regression” equivalent when indicators are categorical?
messages.body_plain:
When indicators are continuous, the function lavPredict() takes input from the “method” argument and, if it was specified as “regression”, changes it to “EBM” before computing factor scores in the lav_predict_eta_normal() function.  The same process takes place when indicators are categorical and “method” is set to “regression”.  Under the hood, the function changes “regression” to “EBM” before computing the factor scores.

The source code (https://rdrr.io/cran/lavaan/src/R/lav_predict.R) for lavPredict() shows how this is done, no matter what type of indicators are being analyzed:

# alias if <https://rdrr.io/r/base/Control.html>(method == "regression") { method <- "ebm" } else <https://rdrr.io/r/base/Control.html> if <https://rdrr.io/r/base/Control.html>(method == "bartlett" || method == "bartlet") { method <- "ml" }

The function lav_predict_eta_normal() is used when the indicators are continuous whereas the lav_predict_eta_ebm_ml() function is used when the indicators are categorical. But before getting to that function, "method" will be saved as “EBM” even if the initial method was “regression”.

What the above tells me is that “regression” factor scores are certainly identical to “EBM” factor scores when indicators are continuous.  Are they also identical when indicators are categorical?  Also, if “regression” is equivalent to “EBM” when indicators are categorical, why does the help page say that “EBM” and “ML” are the options for categorical indicators?

I will note that I found that Muthén indicates that the two methods are equivalent and this is my current understanding (http://www.statmodel.com/discussion/messages/9/397.html): “Mplus uses the regression method (see e.g. Lawley-Maxwell's FA book) - also known as the modal posterior estimator - for continuous outcomes and for categorical outcomes with WLSMV.”

messages.subject_clean: fixed.x = TRUE as the default
messages.body_plain:
The option fixed.x has been discussed a while ago:

https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/Gk93Vp3o5Z0/m/3dWwhLVWBQAJ

This issue came back to me again when working on something else. I understand that, for incremental fit indices such as CFI and TLI, it makes sense to set the covariances between exogenous "x" variables to be free in the baseline model.

However, this can be done without fixed.x = TRUE. Just fit a model with those exogenous "x" variable covariances freely estimated and use this model as the baseline model. There is no need to treat the exogenous "x" variables as fixed variables in the model itself.

Actually, fixed.x = TRUE may not be consistent with other commonly reported results, such as the correlations among the exogenous variables, which researchers usually report their point estimates and p-values and/or confidence intervals. It rarely makes sense to treat these exogenous "x" variables as fixed.

Treating them as fixed can also result in incorrect standard errors for the standardized solution because the sampling error in estimating the population SDs (variances in the model) of the exogenous variables are ignored.

I am not sure about the default behavior of other SEM programs. For AMOS, this is not an issue because users have to manually specify all covariances between exogenous variables, although AMOS uses the independence model as the default. messages.body_plain:
Hello Alexander,

The terms 'regression factors scores' and 'Bartlett factor scores' refer
to the classical approaches to compute factor scores when the indicators
are continuous.

Empirical Bayes Model (EBM) and Maximum Likelihood are 'general'
approaches to assign values to latent variables that work for any type
of indicator (continuous, count, categorical). A nice overview is given
in Chapter 7 of the book

Skrondal, A., & Rabe-Hesketh, S. (2004). Generalized latent variable
modeling: Multilevel, longitudinal, and structural equation models.
Chapman and Hall/CRC.

It turns out that if the items are continuous, EBM == regression, and ML
== Bartlett. That is why lavaan internally uses the more general
concepts of EBM and ML.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
> I'm trying to test a complex model

A path diagram would help communicate what model you are trying to fit.

>           NAS ~ b*RD + f*RD.LHS

RD.LHS cannot be interpreted as an interaction unless both lower-order terms are included.  You only have RD, reflecting the effect of LHS being nested under RD.

http://quantpsy.org/interact/interactions.htm

> the suggestion of doing -1 SD / + 1 SD in the conditional effects (14.81 being the SD of the moderator).

It should be the mean +/- 1 SD from the mean.  Also, you should define conditional specific indirect effects, then define conditional total indirect effects, noting that the moderator affects the size of one of the paths being multiplied (i.e., it is not merely an additive effect; see link above for moderation primer).  Suppose the mean of your moderator is 38:

## specific conditional indirect effects
abc_low  := a*(b + (38 - 14.81)*f)*c
abc_mean := a*(b +  38         *f)*c
abc_high := a*(b + (38 + 14.81)*f)*c
ade_low  := a*(d + (38 - 14.81)*f)*e
ade_mean := a*(d +  38         *f)*e
ade_high := a*(d + (38 + 14.81)*f)*e
## specific total indirect effects
ind_low  := abc_low + ade_low
ind_mean := abc_mean + ade_mean
ind_high := abc_high + ade_high

messages.subject_clean: Nestedness in measurement invariance
messages.body_plain:
Glad you found our multilevel invariance paper, but I would not recommend multilevel SEM for this case.  You specifically want to compare the children's perceptions of their mothers to their perceptions of their fathers.  These are not multiple independent groups.  They are repeated measures of the same child.  So you need to evaluate what is typically called a "longitudinal" measurement invariance, even though it is really just invariance for any kind of dependent "groups" or repeated measures.  Store the data in wide format, with mother variables in different columns than father variables, so there is one row per child.  Then you fit a CFA with separate factors for mothers and fathers, and test whether their measurement parameters are equivalent, similar to the procedure used for testing invariance across groups.  But you have to explicitly use labels to make equality constraints.

>
> Skrondal, A., & Rabe-Hesketh, S. (2004). Generalized latent variable
> modeling: Multilevel, longitudinal, and structural equation models.
> Chapman and Hall/CRC.
>

> == Bartlett. That is why lavaan internally uses the more general

>

> > When indicators are continuous, the function lavPredict() takes input
> > from the “method” argument and, if it was specified as “regression”,
> > changes it to “EBM” before computing factor scores in the
> > lav_predict_eta_normal() function.  The same process takes place when
> > indicators are categorical and “method” is set to “regression”.  Under
> > the hood, the function changes “regression” to “EBM” before computing

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

My question is not very syntax-related, I apologise for that. However, I could not find the answer elsewhere and I hope that some of you could help me understanding my cfa output.

I did a series of model comparisons between nested model (est = MLR). Output from semToos::compareFit shows that the best model is a second-order model. However, some of the item-level loadings are not significant (even if they are > .7) Therefore, I cannot accept this model. I then tried with a bifactor model (but factors were not orthogonalised), and the same happened.

In contrast, the model containing only first-order factors has both loadings and model fit good.

This happens only when std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE. When std.lv <http://std.lv> = FALSE (default) loadings in the second-order and in the bifactor model are significant. However, the estimate variance of 2, out of 7, first-order factors became not significant and very low. The same variances are, instead, significant and explained well (i.e., > .4) when the marker approach is used in the model without the G factor.

I have 6 first-order factors, three items each. The second-order model includes two G factors (three first-order factors load on each of the G factor). N = 400.

Discriminant validity is moderate for two first-order factors (i.e., upper limit cov CFA with std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE is > .8 & < .9). One of these first-order factors is the same that explains negligible variance when setting std.lv <http://std.lv> = FALSE in the second-order model. However, as I said before, the same first-order factor does not have the same problem when the G factors are excluded, regardless of how the model is scaled. Also, I did not see any relevant residual correlations.

Do you have any theoretically explanation, and possibly a reference, for why loadings are not significant when including the G factors? Also, why with nonsignificant loadings the model fit is good?

Thank you all!
Sara


Divide the variance by n, the sample size.
